cases.name: Gather
cases.title: A booking flow, from first choice to change of plan.
cases.summary: Choose a workshop, date and group size, review the details, then manage the saved booking. A complete frontend experience with responsive layouts and local persistence.
cases.unit: steps from choosing a session to reviewing a booking
cases.problem: A registration interface needs more than a successful submit button. People need to understand availability, fix an input, review their choices and change a booking later. The brief was to connect those moments into one usable flow.

decisions.title: Keep the choices visible
decisions.body: Workshop, session, group size and price stay connected throughout the flow. Date labels follow the selected timezone, and unavailable sessions explain their state.

decisions.title: Keep changes attached to their booking
decisions.body: Drafts retain the booking ID and revision when editing, including after a reload. Capacity checks and record changes share a transaction; stale edits from another tab produce a clear message.

decisions.title: Finish the management flow
decisions.body: Saved bookings can be reviewed, edited, cancelled or exported as JSON. Calendar downloads are labelled as demo events. Cancelling returns the places to the local schedule.

try: Pick an available date and two places, then continue with example details.
Review and save the booking. Open Your bookings and change its date or group size.
Reload while editing to resume the draft, then save the changes or cancel the booking.
resume: Built a responsive, accessible booking flow with validation, review, draft recovery and saved booking management.
Implemented transactional local capacity checks, duplicate booking prevention and revision checks for edits from multiple tabs.
cases.boundary: Independent frontend prototype with fictional workshops. Bookings and capacity exist only in this browser; no payment, email or real reservation is made. A live service would need a server, shared inventory and an agreed integration.

cases.name: Current
cases.title: A CSV workspace that keeps the interface usable.
cases.summary: Import, filter and export order data in the browser. A worker handles parsing and queries while a virtual table keeps the visible interface small.
cases.unit: synthetic rows in the reference check
cases.problem: A large CSV can block the interface, and a plausible total can still be wrong. The brief was to make import, inspection and export usable while keeping parsing and arithmetic independently checkable.

decisions.title: Move work off the interface
decisions.body: Parsing and queries run in a dedicated worker. Import can be cancelled, and the table renders a small window of rows rather than the entire dataset.

decisions.title: Reject ambiguous input
decisions.body: The parser handles quoted fields and newlines, validates the fixed schema and dates, and stops on duplicate IDs or malformed amounts. Money is summed in integer cents.

decisions.title: Make output reviewable
decisions.body: Filtered results can be exported. Formula-like text is prefixed for spreadsheet safety, and reference totals are checked independently.

try: Open the demo and generate 100,000 sample rows.
Choose Europe and Direct, then inspect the filtered total.
Export the result; the recorded reference contains 8,263 rows and $4,197,257.69.
resume: Built a React CSV workspace with worker-based parsing and queries, a virtual table, cancellation and filtered export.
Checked 100,000 synthetic records against an independent BigInt reference; browser export was verified with Python csv and Decimal.
cases.boundary: Independent project with synthetic order data. The app does not transmit imported files; data stays in memory and is cleared when leaving the workspace. This is a fixed-schema CSV tool, not a general spreadsheet.

cases.name: Relay
cases.title: Interrupt the worker. Recover the queue.
cases.summary: A browser queue lab that makes interrupted jobs, retries and local effects visible. Crash a worker, reload the page and inspect what recovered.
cases.unit: jobs recovered to 1,000 unique local effects
cases.problem: A worker can stop after claiming a job, and a retry can repeat an effect. The brief was to expose those failure states and recover local work without silently duplicating ledger entries.

decisions.title: Use expiring ownership
decisions.body: Jobs are claimed atomically with a lease and token. Expired jobs can be reclaimed; a stale token cannot finish work after ownership changes.

decisions.title: Commit related state together
decisions.body: A local effect and job completion share one IndexedDB transaction. Injected write failures must roll back both changes.

decisions.title: Make recovery observable
decisions.body: The interface exposes attempts, leases and effects, with controls to terminate the worker and export the ledger for inspection.

try: Create a 1,000-job batch and start the worker.
Crash the worker while jobs are running, then reload.
After leases expire, restart and export the ledger to inspect unique effects.
resume: Implemented atomic job claims, expiring leases, stale-token rejection and transactional local effects in IndexedDB.
Recorded an Edge run recovering 1,000 jobs after worker termination and reload, with exactly 1,000 unique local effects.
cases.boundary: At-least-once execution with deduplicated local ledger effects. This does not guarantee exactly-once effects in external APIs. An open page and retained browser storage are required.

cases.name: HALO
cases.title: A product scene with choices that travel.
cases.summary: Configure a pendant light and share its settings, or open your own GLB in the companion model workspace. Inspect original materials, fit the view and export a PNG.
cases.unit: configuration combinations checked for URL round trips
cases.problem: An attractive 3D scene is only part of a configurator. Controls need to change the object, shared links need to restore the same choices, and people without WebGL still need a useful page.

decisions.title: Connect controls to the scene
decisions.body: Procedural geometry, rendered materials, diameter and light color respond to configuration state. Camera and rotation controls let visitors inspect the result.

decisions.title: Validate the shared state
decisions.body: Only supported finite values enter the scene. URL decoding rejects unknown finishes and out-of-range settings; zero brightness survives a round trip.

decisions.title: Keep an accessible fallback
decisions.body: Responsive controls and specification export remain available without WebGL. Reduced-motion preferences disable automatic rotation.

decisions.title: Work with supplied product assets
decisions.body: The companion model workspace loads self-contained GLB files in the browser, preserves their materials and fits different proportions to the camera. Two original downloadable objects make the flow usable immediately. New files replace the scene only after loading successfully.

try: Choose a finish and diameter, then change brightness.
Share the configuration and reopen its URL.
Save the JSON specification and compare it with the restored controls.
Open the model workspace, switch between the two sample objects, or open a local GLB and save its view.
resume: Built a responsive Three.js configurator with procedural geometry, live material controls, shareable URLs, PNG and JSON export.
Verified 900 configuration round trips, including zero brightness; added input bounds, reduced-motion behavior and a WebGL fallback.
cases.boundary: Independent product concept, with no checkout or calibrated light simulation. The model workspace displays a static view of uncompressed GLB files up to 20 MB with embedded textures. Uploaded files remain in memory; the sample objects are original code-built geometry.

cases.name: Field
cases.title: A living pattern, with a numerical check.
cases.summary: Paint into a Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion field, adjust parameters and export the result. Compare the GPU implementation with a CPU reference in the browser.
cases.unit: concentrations compared in the live GPU check
cases.problem: A generated pattern can look convincing even when a GPU update is incorrect. The brief was to combine an expressive drawing surface with a small, reproducible numerical comparison.

decisions.title: Advance the field on the GPU
decisions.body: Two floating-point render targets alternate reading and writing. A nine-point Laplacian and periodic boundaries define the update.

decisions.title: Compare against a reference
decisions.body: A live check advances a seeded 64 by 64 field for 20 steps on the GPU and CPU, compares 8,192 concentrations, and reports the observed maximum absolute error.

decisions.title: Respect the viewing context
decisions.body: The simulation pauses when hidden or off screen and starts paused for reduced motion. PNG export captures the current field.

try: Open the studio and choose a pattern preset.
Paint into the surface and adjust the parameters.
Run the GPU check and download the observed result; the pass threshold is 0.0005.
resume: Implemented a Gray-Scott studio with floating-point GPU ping-pong targets, seeded drawing, parameter controls and PNG export.
Added a live GPU/CPU comparison over 8,192 concentrations, plus equilibrium, boundary and stability tests.
cases.boundary: A dimensionless visual simulation, not a calibrated chemical model. WebGL 2 and floating-point render targets are required. The numerical check reports the visitor's actual graphics context.

cases.name: Invoice Gate
cases.title: Valid JSON can still be the wrong invoice.
cases.summary: A runnable Python example and accompanying article about the checks between extracted invoice data and a SQLite ledger.
cases.unit: tests covering validation, retries and import transactions
cases.problem: Extracted fields can satisfy a JSON schema while the arithmetic is wrong. The article starts with a synthetic invoice that is off by twenty cents, then explains how to stop that inconsistency before import.

decisions.title: Start with a concrete failure
decisions.body: The explanation follows one incorrect total from line items to tax and total, making the validation problem easy to reproduce.

decisions.title: Keep parsing decisions explicit
decisions.body: A trusted number-format setting controls parsing. Decimal text becomes integer minor units, and original extracted strings remain available for review.

decisions.title: Explain retries and limits
decisions.body: Identical retries return duplicate; changed content needs review. Batch conflicts roll back the transaction. The article distinguishes arithmetic consistency from approval.

try: Read the article's twenty-cent mismatch example.
Clone the repository and run python demo.py (Python 3.12+).
Run python -m unittest -v, then inspect the retry and conflicting-batch cases.
resume: Wrote a code-led article explaining invoice arithmetic, explicit number formats, retry handling and transactional SQLite imports.
Built the companion Python CLI with 20 tests, including conflicting revisions, rollback and concurrent imports; no external packages required.
cases.boundary: Independent writing sample with synthetic data. The project starts after extraction; it contains no OCR engine or payment connection. Consistent arithmetic does not mean an invoice is authentic or approved.

cases.name: PROOF
cases.title: Grade the resulting state, then inspect the trace.
cases.summary: A small order-fulfilment simulator for exploring agent tool-use failures, recorded actions and recovery. Imported traces are replayed and graded again.
cases.unit: public scenarios, with six seeded variants each
cases.problem: A plausible action trace does not establish that an order was fulfilled. Lost acknowledgements and stock conflicts make it useful to inspect final state and distinguish justified handoff from autonomous completion.

decisions.title: Keep the environment bounded
decisions.body: Four public conditions cover normal execution, a lost acknowledgement, inventory conflict and required handoff. A session permits at most 16 accepted world actions.

decisions.title: Recompute the result
decisions.body: Imported actions replay against the versioned simulator. The grader checks orders and constraints rather than trusting supplied scores or one exact action path.

decisions.title: Keep provenance visible
decisions.body: Reference policies and recorded agent trials are labelled separately. The recording retains failed submissions alongside successful actions, and unknown usage stays unknown.

try: Open the lab and compare the reference policies.
Choose the lost-acknowledgement scenario and inspect final order state.
Replay a recorded trial and inspect the action trace and separate handoff result.
resume: Built a seeded agent evaluation simulator with bounded actions, final-state grading and replay verification of imported traces.
Documented four public scenarios with six variants each, separating reference policies, recorded agent trials and justified handoffs.
cases.boundary: Synthetic, public demonstration cases. This is not a general model ranking or production reliability benchmark. Replaying a trace verifies its consequences in the simulator, not the model's identity.
